list.listitem: There are many conditions (eg, cancer, end-stage heart disease), where it is reasonable to help patients and their families prepare for dying.C
Accurate and timely communication with patients and families and attention to physical, psychological, and spiritual support is essential for excellent care.B

Two broad types of documents are useful in advance care planning—living wills and proxy designation.C Living wills do not require specific forms (although many states have them), but proxy designations (durable power of attorney for health care) require legal documentation.C Educational interventions may assist in completion of these documents.B
Common physical and psychological symptoms reported by dying patients include constipation, fatigue and weakness, confusion, dyspnea, depression, and pain.B
A stepwise approach to pain should be used beginning with nonopioids, increasing to mild opioids, and then stronger opioids (including round the clock approaches) as needed.B

Palliative care should be considered for patients with major illness or chronic complex disease that negatively affects their quality of life (QOL), particularly when they experience significant disease symptoms that are stressful and the patient and family caregivers need supportive care; care may be paid for by personal insurance and partially by Medicaid and Medicare. Hospice care should be considered early in the dying process and is usually a covered benefit of Medicare.C

Telehospice is a way to continue to provide end-of-life care virtually during the pandemic and may be applicable to other situations when in person care is not possible. It was non-inferior in a RCT. C

Based on National Center for Health Statistics, there were there were 3,383,729 deaths (1,027 deaths per 100,000 population) in the United States in 2020 compared to approximately 2.8 million deaths in the United States in 2017 (863.8 deaths per 100,000 population).

The age-adjusted death rate in 2017 was higher for the non-Hispanic black versus non-Hispanic white population (881 deaths per 100,000 vs. 755 deaths per 100,000). Age-adjusted death rates for other populations are lower than for whites.
Average life expectancy decreased from 78.8 years in 2019 to 77 years in 2020; 79.9 years for females and 74.2 years for males.
Infant mortality statistics showed a decrease from 6.9 deaths per 1000 live births in 2005 to 5.66 deaths per 1000 live births in 2018 and 5.42 per 1000 live births in 2020.

Data from over 1.3 million Medicare fee-for-service decedents showed that the proportion of deaths occurring in acute care hospitals decreased from 32.6% in 2000 to 19.8% in 2015. In 2015, 40.1% of deaths occurred in a home or community setting, including assisted living facilities; this increased from 30.7% in 2000.
In 2018, there were about 1.6 million patients enrolled in hospice care within 4700 agencies, based on data from the CDC; 66.4% of these agencies are under for-profit ownership.

According to the National Hospice and Palliative Care Organization about 1.55 million Medicare beneficiaries were enrolled in hospice care for one day or more in 2018, a 4% increase from the prior year. About 55% of hospice patients were female. The age distribution of Medicare hospice patients was as follows: <65 years:16.3%, 65-74 years: 22.3%, 75-84 years: 28%, and >85 years: 33.4%. Caucasian/White patients were the majority of Medicare hospice patients in 2018 (82%).

The leading causes of death per 100,000 population in 2020 were cardiovascular disease (168.2) and cancer (144.1). COVID-19 became the third leading cause of death (85). The remaining 7 leading causes of death were unintentional injuries (57.6), stroke (38.8), chronic lower respiratory diseases (36.4), Alzheimer’s disease (32.4), diabetes (24.8), influenza and pneumonia (13), kidney diseases (nephritis, nephrotic syndrome and nephrosis; 12.7). These 10 causes of death accounted for 74.1% of the deaths in 2020.

Among infant deaths, the leading causes were congenital malformations, low birth weight, sudden infant death syndrome, unintentional injuries, maternal complications, cord and placental complications, bacterial sepsis of newborn, respiratory distress of newborn, diseases of the circulatory system, and neonatal hemorrhage which accounted for 67.5% of all infant deaths in the United States.

According to the CDC, coronavirus (COVID)-19 caused 341,199 deaths among 19,663,976 cases (1.73%) in the US in 2020 and about 1,8 million deaths worldwide. Of those infected, approximately 85% experience a mild illness and 15% experience severe disease requiring hospitalization, including 5% who require ICU admission. The overall infection-fatality rate is estimated to be 0.66% and the overall case-fatality rate (CFR, identified as infected) is 1.38%. The CFR increases from 0.06% for those in their 20’s to 0.15% in their 30’s, 0.30% in their 40’s, 1.3% in their 50’s, 4.0% in their 60’s, 8.6% in their 70’s, and 13.4% for those 80 and older. Mortality rates for the 1151 patients (20.2%) with COVID-19 requiring mechanical ventilation in a NYC study were 76.4% among those 18-65 years and 97.2% for those older than age 65 years.
Causes of death are multifactorial.

The major modifiable contributors to death are tobacco use, high fat diet, physical inactivity, alcohol use, motor vehicle accidents, incidents involving firearms, high-risk sexual behaviors, illicit drug use, and microbial and toxic agents.

Actively dying is the time leading up to death and is associated with a well-recognized pattern of signs and symptoms. It can range from 24 hours up to longer than 14 days. Signs include irregular breathing, hypotension, mottled skin and cool extremities, and altered consciousness/coma. Symptoms include loss of appetite; hallucinations, delirium or agitation; and incontinence of bladder and/or bowel. End-of-life care providers should recognize the stages of actively to provide the proper management and guide patients and their families.

The European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) 2021 guidelines note that early signs that can be present more than 1 week before death in advanced cancer patients include reduced conscious state, Palliative Performance Scale of 20% (i.e., bed-bound, completely dependent, food intake minimal-to-none) and dysphagia for liquids. Late signs increasing the likelihood of death within 3 days include non-reactive pupils, radial artery pulselessness, low urine output of <100 ml in 12 hours, inability to close eyelids, Cheyne-Stokes respiration, and vocal-fold grunting.

Guidelines for end-of-life care (based on systematic review) have been published by the American College of Physicians (ACP, 2019). The provision of end-of-life care including good symptom control; ongoing commitment to serve the patient and family; and physical, psychological, and spiritual support are ethical imperatives and the hallmarks of high-quality end-of-life and hospice care provided by a team of health professionals. ACP recommends patient and family preparation about the course of illness and care options; regular patient assessment and treatment for pain, dyspnea, and depression; and routinely raising advanced planning with patients.
Patients entering the terminal stage of their lives should have access to all required care, management and support. This care should be provided with full respect to patient dignity.
Providers of palliative care for dying patients must be updated with all necessary clinical, ethical, and legal information about used interventions.

Guidelines for care of adult cancer patients at the end of life are also available from ESMO, 2021. This guideline covers goal setting within three categories of rationalizing treatments, managing symptoms, and providing multidisciplinary care. Recommendations are evidence-based, when possible, and were compiled by a multidisciplinary group of experts.

Authors of a systematic review of end-of-life programs that had a significant positive effect on any outcome measured found that the most common shared features were linkage with acute care, multidisciplinary nature, end-of-life expertise and training, holistic care, pain and symptom management, and professional psychosocial support. Features shared by interventions that produced cost reductions were linkage, around-the-clock availability, and customized care planning
Guidance is also offered for pediatric palliative cancer care, as much of this care occurs outside of the hospital and only adult hospice care providers may be available.
Recommendations for specific end-of-life care pathways can’t be made due to lack of available evidence on important patient and relative outcomes.

In a study of attributes of a "good death," 6 major components emerged: adequate pain and symptom management; patient participation in decision making; greater preparation for the end of life; a feeling of meaningfulness at the end of life; the ability to contribute to the well-being of others; and affirming the patient as a unique and whole person.

The ACP Ethics Manual, Seventh edition, notes that adult patient with or without decision-making capacities have the right to make decisions to accept or refuse life-sustaining treatments. Psychiatric consultation should be made for patients with mental illnesses or impairment to evaluate their ability to make decisions.

listitem.strong: Recognition of last days of life

list.listitem: Recognition of patients going into the dying process can be difficult. The patient should be evaluated for deterioration in certain symptoms including loss of appetite, level of consciousness, and progression of fatigue. (See pathophysiology above.)
Tools are available that promote shared decision-making with patients with serious illness that appear to improve advance care planning documentation, clinical decisions, and treatment received.

For example, in an RCT of 246 patients ≥64 years of age with heart failure and an estimated likelihood of death of >50% within 2 years, use of a video-assisted intervention and advance care planning checklist compared to verbal information only improved knowledge and decisions towards comfort care rather than life-prolonging care.

In another RCT of patients with advanced cancer, a web-based self-care intervention combined with care coordinator visits and telephone follow-up was compared with usual care. It reduced patient depression, pain and fatigue and improved quality of life. It also reduced stress and depression for caregivers at 6 months.

Palliative care is not the same as hospice care. Palliative care is provided to any patient (not necessary dying) and aims to alleviate patient suffering. Palliative care can be provided alongside the curative therapy. Hospice care is provided to dying patients given a prognosis of death within 6 months when curative treatment is no longer effective, and also aims to alleviate suffering. Hospice care can be considered a subset of palliative care.

There are 5 basic principles of palliative care: (1) respecting the goals, preferences, and choices of the dying person; (2) caring for the person's medical, emotional, social, and spiritual needs; (3) supporting the needs of family members; (4) helping with access to needed medical healthcare; and (5) providing excellent care at the end of life.

Indications for referral to palliative care are not well delineated. Authors of a comprehensive review suggested that a person can be eligible for palliative care if they have a major illness or chronic complex disease that negatively affects QOL and/or the patient has a disease or significant disease symptoms that are stressful for the patient and the caregiver, and the patient needs supportive treatment for the curative disease. Referral is prompted by situations such as deterioration of disease status, decreased mobility, oxygen dependency, or progressive weight loss, or for patients with diseases that can progress rapidly to death as heart failure, chronic obstructive lung disease or cancer.

Authors of a systematic review of indications for referral to palliative care for patients with dementia identified 13 categories of referral criteria, including disease-based and needs-based criteria. The most commonly discussed criterion was dementia stage (advanced or new; n = 43, 73%) followed by medical complications of dementia such as pneumonia, falls or decubitus ulcers (n = 12, 20%), and poor prognosis (less than 2 years life expectancy; n = 11, 19%).

Use of the Surprise Question ("Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months?") in primary care settings has good positive predictive value (33%), with a sensitivity and specificity for actual death within one year of 50% and 99%, respectively (positive likelihood ratio [LR+] 50; negative likelihood ratio [LR−] 0.50), and should prompt consideration of a palliative-care referral. Use of the Supportive and Palliative Care Indicators Tool (SPICT) is more sensitive (58% vs 50%) but more time-consuming to implement.

Similar to late referral into hospice care, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 169 studies from 23 countries, involving 11,996,479 patients, found that the median duration from initiation of palliative care to death was 18.9 days. The authors note that this timeframe is much shorter than the time needed to achieve full benefits of multidisciplinary team-based palliative care.

strong.em: Reduced costs attributed to palliative care

list.listitem: Non-essential medications should be considered for discontinuation. In a RCT of 381 patients in palliative care who were on statins, there was no difference in death within 60 days among the 189 patients randomized to discontinuing statins and few experienced cardiovascular events. In addition, total quality of life (QOL) was improved for those discontinuing statins and the mean cost savings were $716 per patient.

In one study using 6 samples including 133,118 patients, a palliative care consultation that was conducted in 3.6% reduced hospital costs by -$3237 with greater cost reduction among those with a cancer diagnosis. In another trial of 199 medical ICU patients, those randomized to an early-triggered palliative care consultation vs. usual care were transitioned earlier and significantly more often to do-not-resuscitate/do-not-intubate orders (50.5% vs. 23.4%) and to hospice care (18.6% vs. 4.9%), and had less ICU and post-ICU healthcare resource use. There were no differences in ICU or hospital length of stay, in-hospital mortality (22.6% vs. 29.4%), or 30-day mortality (35.1% vs. 36.3%) between groups.

In a cluster randomized trial conducted in 73 European long-term care facilities, the Palliative Care for Older People (PACE) Steps to Success' intervention, a 1-year palliative care program to integrate general palliative care into day-to-day routines, significantly reduced costs in the intervention group by €983.28, primarily from decreased hospitalization-related costs.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 trials with 13,664 patients with primarily non-cancer illness, found that palliative care, compared with usual care, was significantly associated with less acute healthcare use and modestly lower symptom burden, but no difference in QOL.

There is controversy over the benefits of palliative care provision. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 palliative-care trials with over 12,000 patients found improvements in patient QOL and symptom burden but no clinically-meaningful benefit when only studies with low risk of bias were considered. In this review, there was also no significant association between palliative care and survival; evidence for reducing overall health care expenditures, and improving caregiver QOL and satisfaction was mixed.

The setting of care provision is likely important. Within ambulatory care settings, authors of a meta-analysis of 14 studies including 2,934 patients comparing integrating palliative care to usual care found no differences on patient health-related QOL, patient depressive symptom scores or patient satisfaction. Palliative care models were more effective for increasing advance directive documentation (RR 1.62, 95% CI 1.35 to 1.94).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 42 RCTs, including 6678 patients and 1101 caregivers/family members, found that hospital-based palliative care resulted in improved health-related QOL (small effect size of 0.26 SMD over usual care, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.37, I2 = 3%, 10 studies with 1344 participants, low-quality evidence), reduced symptom burden (-0.26 SMD over usual care, 95% CI -0.41 to -0.12, I2 = 0%, 6 studies with 761 participants, very low-quality evidence) and improved patient satisfaction with care. Intervention patients were also more likely to die at home. Although study data were limited, there were no observed differences in pain or caregiver burden. No serious harms were reported in 8 studies. Cost-effectiveness results were inconsistent.

Among patients with advanced cancer, palliative compared to usual care improved QOL at 4-7 months based on 19 reports but effects may not last as there was no significant difference in 4 reports at 10 or more months of follow-up.

A nurse-led, palliative care-focused intervention and care coordination provided concurrently with oncology care was associated with higher QOL and mood scores compared with usual care in one RCT. There were no differences in symptom intensity scores or reduced days in the hospital, or ICU or emergency department visits.

Provision of inpatient palliative-care services for patients who received stem cell transplantation led to a smaller decrease in QOL, which persisted for up to 3 months in one RCT. In an RCT of hospitalized patients receiving palliative care, patients and their primary family caregivers randomized to family meetings had reduced family caregiver distress and enhanced preparedness for their caregiving role. No differences were observed in quality of end-of-life care or healthcare utilization.

In another RCT of 461 patients randomized to at least monthly consultation and follow-up by a palliative care team or standard cancer care, there were no significant differences in the primary QOL measure. There were significant differences favoring the intervention group in satisfaction with care.

In nursing homes, Palliative Care Needs Rounds - monthly hour-long staff-only triage meetings to discuss residents at risk of dying without a plan in place - improved staff self-reported capacity and perceptions of quality of resident’s death and dying in a RCT of 12 care homes in Australia. In another cluster-RCT in 78 nursing homes in 7 countries, however, there was no improvement in staff knowledge, resident’s comfort in the last week of life, or health-related QOL in homes randomized to use of the Palliative Care for Older People (PACE) Steps to Success Program compared to usual care. There was an improvement in quality of death, which covers quality of care and quality of dying items.
In-home, community case conferences for patients with advanced fibrotic interstitial lung disease improved palliative symptoms and QOL after 4 weeks in one small trial.

The possibility of combining chemotherapy (or other interventions) with supportive care is increasingly being explored. For example, a systematic review of 16 RCTs with 2714 patients found improved survival when chemotherapy was added to supportive care. ESMO guidelines (2021) recommend against using chemotherapy and immunotherapy in the last weeks of life due to adverse effects and limited benefit but suggest that single-fraction radiation therapy may provide effective symptomatic relief for metastatic bone pain within 2 weeks, or tumor-related bleeding within 2 days.

The concept of advance directives/advance care planning should be introduced. This refers to decisions that a patient makes regarding the management and care that they want to receive during serious or chronic illness. These decisions are based on a patient’s values, beliefs, and preferences. ACP includes continuous and updated discussions with patients and their families, as well as documentation of proposed treatments. Possible scenarios can be discussed such as recovery from an acute event (specifying acceptable interventions) and persistent vegetative state (preferences for life-sustaining interventions).

The National Hospice and Palliative Care Organization provides guidance for patients and caregivers for ACP. Reimbursement to health care providers for ACP counseling was approved by Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).
Recommendations for ACP in adults with congenital heart disease that cover staged implementation of ACPs and overcoming barriers to ACP are also provided by the European Society of Cardiology.

In an RCT of 165 patients with advanced COPD, a nurse-led 1.5-hour session on advanced care planning increased these discussions with physicians without increasing patient distress and reduced anxiety in loved ones.

End-of-life discussions in a cohort study of patients with advanced cancer and their caregivers were associated with less aggressive medical care near death and earlier hospice referrals. In contrast, aggressive care is associated with poorer patient QOL and worse bereavement adjustment for caregivers.

Not all patients will be receptive to ACP; in one study, higher level of religious coping in patients with advanced cancer was significantly associated with less ACP and increased use of life-prolonging care in the last week of life. It is possible that patients with high religious coping were less likely to be offered ACP. In addition, strong religious belief in miracles, present in 46% (73/158) of patients in one study, was associated with diminished impact of receiving news of cancer progression on change in prognostic understanding. Interestingly, in a secondary analysis of an RCT of palliative care in patients with advanced cancer, hope scores, measured by the Herth Hope Index, did not differ between patients who had an end-of-life discussion and those who did not.

Despite proposed benefits, the frequency of providing effective ACP in clinical practice are still considered low. Authors of a systematic review of 20 studies including patients primarily in later stages of illness found an ACP participation refusal rate, based on 8 studies, of 36% (206/579 patients) although only 5% had refused due to lack of readiness or upset with the word “palliative”.

Barriers to discussing and completing advance directives include perceptions by physicians or family that patients are not "absolutely, hopelessly ill," vague directives, and unavailable or overwhelmed family members.Also, patient-related barriers include fears of being engaged in discussions about their approaching death which were described as informative but also distressful and difficult.

Although there are cultural differences in desire for information about death, most older patients (88%) in 1 survey wanted to be told when they have cancer.Korean, Mexican, Japanese, and Native Americans are more likely to discourage discussion of terminal illness and prognosis with patients and prefer that only families be informed.
There are limited data regarding advance directives in patients with severe mental illness; the data suggest that the use of a directive does not adversely affect care decisions for these patients.

Without ACP planning, surrogates may be consulted for decision making for end-of-life care when the patient can no longer speak for themselves. In 1 study, surrogates made end-of-life treatment decisions that reflected the desires of the terminally ill patient only two thirds of the time.Asking patients both in advance and, if possible, during a serious illness about their preferences for resuscitation ventilator use, and feeding is the best option; preferences sometimes change.

These are two broad types of documents that are useful in advance care planning: living wills and proxy designation. Although 80% of Americans endorse completing living wills, only about 36.7% have completed an advance directive, including 29.3% with living wills, based on a systematic review of 150 US studies published between 2011-2016 and including 795,909 people. In the Health and Retirement Study, of 6,122 patients over age 60 years who died between 2000 and 2010, the proportion who had advanced directives increased from 47% to 72%.

The proxy designation durable power of attorney for health care requires legal documentation. The US Supreme Court has ruled that patients have a right to decide about refusing or terminating medical interventions.

strong.em: Interventions to increase uptake of ACP documents

list.listitem: In a clustered RCT of 201 modestly frail elderly patients, a single intensive advance care planning intervention of 2 hours duration on average, including travel time, dramatically increased the completion an advance directive at the end of 1 year (93% vs. 34% in the control group; NNT = 2) and the increased identification of surrogate decision makers (94% vs. 67%; NNT = 4).

In an RCT of 205 hospitalized patients, randomization to a single discussion of preferences for end-of-life care did not result in a significant difference in fulfillment of preferred place of death over usual care (52% vs. 35%) or in amount of time spent in hospital among the 111 deceased patients (23% vs. 49%); however, more patients in the intervention group died at home (40% vs. 17%).

In the nursing home setting, authors of a meta-analysis of 9 trials including 2905 patients advance care planning interventions significantly increased documentation of end-of-life care preferences (OR 1.95, 95% CI 1.64, 2.32), but not satisfaction with end-of-life care from families' perspectives.
Increasing uptake of ACPs has also been demonstrated using games.

The PREPARE online module helps patients make decisions and prepare an advanced directive. In one RCT of 986 English-speaking or Spanish-speaking primary care patients, access to this online module plus a form was more effective than providing the form alone in documenting advance directives within 15 months (43% vs. 33.1%, respectively; NNT = 10).

Efficient management of symptoms should be provided for patients’ as they progress into the dying process. Alternative routes of drug administration such as sublingual, rectal, and transdermal should be considered in patients suffering from swallowing problems. Medical staff working with patients with end-stage disease should be competent in basic palliative care.

In addition, clinicians treating patients in the emergency department can also contribute to palliative care through screening, discussions with patients and their families, symptom management, transitions across care settings, end-of-lfe care, and education and support.

Pain is very common occurring in approximately in 50% in patients at their last month of life. Pain management includes nonpharmacologic treatment, pain medications, and other palliative procedures (). A stepwise approach to pain should be used beginning with nonopioids and increasing to mild opioids or stronger opioids as needed. Dosing frequency is more important for onset of analgesia than the starting dose.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released updated guidelines for prescribing opioids for chronic pain in 2016, which were updated in 2022. The recommendations, however, do not apply to pain related to sickle cell disease or cancer or to patients receiving palliative or end-of-life care. Overall, the guidelines recommend that clinicians maximize use of nonopioid therapy, use opioids only when benefits outweigh risks, establish treatment goals and discontinuation plans with patients prior to opioid use, and prescribe the lowest effective dosage. Most of the specific recommendations for dosing refer to patients with acute and chronic pain who are not receiving end-of-life or palliative care. Opioid options include fentanyl, morphine, oxycodone, and hydromorphone. Opioids and their metabolites are excreted renally and may accumulate in terminally-ill patients causing confusion, drowsiness and hallucinations. Fentanyl and methadone have inactive metabolites and only small amounts of unaltered drug are excreted through the kidneys

The usual analgesic effect of morphine ranges from 6 hours to 2.3 days. NICE guidelines recommend an initial dose of 20 to 30 mg oral morphine daily and titrating as needed (eg, 10-15 mg oral SR morphine twice daily). Transdermal patches are also an option, for example fentanyl 12 mcg patch which is equivalent to 45 mg oral morphine daily. ESMO, 2021, recommends immediate-release sublingual, subcutaneous or IV opioids for those in a pain crisis in the last few days of life to ensure faster pain control. For advanced cancer patients, they also recommend continuous subcutaneous infusion as the preferred route of drug administration for most patients via a cannula in situ, most commonly in the sub-clavicular and abdominal areas, that can be left in place for a maximum of 7 days (usually 3-5 days).

Round-the-clock dosing is used for continuous pain. Rescue medication is added if needed, usually 10% to 15% of the 24-hour total morphine dose repeated every hour if necessary. The daily dose can be increased by the total dose of rescue medication used the previous day.

Pain should be assessed frequently and, if not well controlled, the dose of morphine can be increased by 50% for moderate and 100% for severe pain. The daily dose needed to manage pain effectively is typically between 100 mg and 250 mg of morphine. The optimal dose of morphine is the dose that brings complete pain relief without side effects (no ceiling dose).
Sustained-release morphine does not appear to be useful in patients with severe stable COPD who have no signs of hypoxia, CHF, or CO2 retention.
NICE guidelines provide a pathway for managing opioids in palliative care patients, supportive and palliative care in adults, and end of life care for adults.

listitem.strong: Alternate or adjunctive treatment for pain

list.listitem: A team approach to assistance with pain may be useful; in one RCT, patients working with the assistance team (mean 10.6 contacts) showed modest but greater improvements in pain-related disability and depression severity than usual care. Authors of a systematic review of 13 RCTs of team approaches to pain management found a clinically meaningful improvement in 8 of at least one patient-reported pain outcome. In particular, a care manager was a common structural feature of the interventions with some clinical effect on patient-reported pain.
Acupuncture can be useful for reducing pain.

In one RCT of simple touch versus massage therapy for patients with moderate to severe pain, both groups demonstrated immediate improvement in pain and mood but massage was superior for both. There were no other differences between groups including sustained pain, worst pain, analgesic use, or QOL.

Constipation: This is often due to medications, inactivity, and poor nutritional/hydration status. Options are presented in . Senna and stool softeners are useful for prevention. Authors of a Cochrane review found five studies of lactulose, senna, co-danthramer, misrakasneham, docusate, and magnesium hydroxide. They concluded that the interventions appeared to be similarly effective.

Methylnaltrexone be helpful for opioid-induced constipation that doesn’t respond to traditional preventive laxatives and was useful for laxation at the end of life in a combined RCT of 287 patients (OR 7.0 for stool at 4 hours).

Intestinal obstruction: Authors of a Cochrane review identified 43 studies of surgery for patients with intestinal obstruction due to GI and gynecologic malignancies. These were mostly retrospective reviews that reported clinical resolution rates from 27% to 68% (most often using ability to feed orally as the key outcome). Rates of reobstruction varied greatly from 0% to 63%, as did rates of operative complications and mortality.

A Cochrane review comparing surgical with medical management in patients with bowel obstruction in ovarian cancer identified only a single retrospective observational study with 47 subjects. The authors concluded that surgery was more effective at prolonging life, but the quality of evidence is very low and the magnitude of benefit was not described.

Nausea and vomiting: This can be induced by recent chemotherapy or radiation therapy, constipation, obstruction, psychological causes (anxiety, fear), biochemical causes (e.g., hypercalcemia, hyponatremia, uremia), increased intracranial pressure, vestibular dysfunction, excessive cough, ascites, and gastroparesis. Treat the underlying cause when possible. Serotonin or olanzapine may be helpful. Although anti-dopamine agents (eg, haloperidol, risperidone, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) can also be useful, authors of a Cochrane review found a single RCT comparing haloperidol/lorazepam/diphenhydramine gel with 22 patients. It was no better than placebo.

ESMO guidelines (2021) recommend metoclopramide as the drug of choice for nausea and vomiting in advanced cancer patients. This drug should be used with caution in patients with partial bowel obstruction and not used if complete bowel obstruction is present. Switching to subcutaneous administration may be helpful for opioid-induced nausea and vomiting. Drugs with an antidopaminergic mode of action (e.g. haloperidol, metoclopramide) and serotonin 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor antagonists (e.g. ondansetron, palonosetron) may be effective in patients with opioid-induced emesis based on weak evidence.
Second-line medication for refractory symptoms include anticholinergics, corticosteroids, and cannabinoid agents.
For dyspnea, when possible treat reversible causes such as infection or hypoxia. Options are shown in .

ESMO guidelines (2021) note that breathlessness is highly prevalent in advanced cancer patients, affecting between 20% and 70%, and is associated with poor prognosis. Screening for breathlessness should be conducted monitoring both intensity, for example using a numeric scale, and for functional impact using an objective measure such as the modified Medical Research Council breathlessness scale.

Authors of a Cochrane review confirmed the benefit of oral or parenteral opioids to relieve breathlessness, although numbers of patients in studies were small. Opioids at appropriate doses may reduce the sense of air hunger in patients without accelerating death, and sublingual and concentrated forms of morphine and oxycodone are available. ESMO guidelines recommend starting with daily dose morphine SR 10-20 mg over 24 hours for opioid-naive patients. For opioid-tolerant patients, an increase in of 25%-50% in baseline opioid dose may be considered for the relief of cancer-related breathlessness.

In a multisite Australian RCT of 248 adults with chronic breathlessness, however, there were no differences in breathlessness for patients randomized to regular, low-dose (20 mg daily), sustained-release morphine compared with placebo, although patients in the intervention arm used less rescue immediate-release morphine.
A single session of breathing training may be helpful.

Oxygen delivered by high-flow nasal cannula was superior to conventional oxygen therapy in reducing dyspnea severity in the first hour of treatment in an RCT of 44 patients with do-not-intubate status and hypoxemic respiratory failure presenting to an ED in Thailand. ESMO guidelines recommend against use of palliative oxygen in patients with a SpO2 >90%.

Quantifying dyspnea at end of life is challenging as most patients can’t report symptoms. For patients who are non-communicative, heart rate, neck muscle use during inspiration, abdominal paradox, facial expression of fear, and supplemental oxygen correlate with patient-reported dyspnea, although it is not clear that intervention based on these criteria will be helpful.

Authors of a Cochrane review of benzodiazepines as a treatment for breathlessness near the end of life concluded that there was no clear evidence for or against their benefit based on 8 studies with 214 patients. They should be considered a second- or third-line drug for breathlessness in this setting. In a pilot study of patients with breathlessness primarily from COPD or interstitial lung disease, use of mirtazapine reduced worst breathlessness ratings at day 28 compared to placebo. ESMO guidelines (2021) however, suggest consideration of benzodiazepines in cancer patients with breathlessness associated with anxiety. In individuals suffering from refractory breathlessness, midazolam infusion may be considered as palliative sedation.

Delirium can be secondary to metabolic abnormalities, infection, brain tumors, medications, and multiple other causes. Reversible causes should be identified and managed. If a reversible cause cannot be identified and treated, consider use of a medication listed in .
ESMO guidelines (2021) suggest consideration of olanzapine or quetiapine for symptomatic management of delirium in advanced cancer patients.

Investigators using a large well-designed RCT compared risperidone, haloperidol, and placebo in 247 hospitalized cancer patients in palliative care who were experiencing delirium. Overall survival was worse in the haloperidol group, and those taking active drug had worse delirium symptoms at day 3. In another RCT, combination lorazepam plus haloperidol was more effective in improving comfort than haloperidol alone for patients with agitated delirium with no differences in delirium-related distress or survival.
Severe refractory agitation can be managed by palliative sedation and the induction of unconsciousness.

Fatigue: This can be caused by underlying disease (eg, heart failure), cachexia, dehydration, anemia, hypothyroidism, and/or medications. See for treatment options. Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to recommend any particular drug, with the best evidence available for modafinil and methylphenidate. Oral melatonin did not improve fatigue in patients with advanced cancer in one small study. In one pilot study, acupressure vs. sham acupressure was useful in reducing fatigue in patients with lung cancer. ESMO guidelines (2021) recommend short-term use of dexamethasone or methylprednisolone, however, use of corticosteroids is contraindicated in patients with delirium or approaching imminent death.

Depression: This can be difficult to diagnose because many of the somatic symptoms used to diagnose depression in healthy individuals are present in patients who are dying; psychological criteria become more important for treatment decisions. If medication is initiated, low doses should be used initially ().

Anxiety: No data were available on management of anxiety in terminally-ill patients. In a systematic review of 3 small RCTs, investigators concluded that the addition of aromatherapy to massage alone did not improve anxiety for patients receiving palliative care.

Nutrition and hydration: Reduced oral intake is common. Authors of a Cochrane review found no evidence that medically-assisted hydration prolongs life, but could not rule out a benefit based on the scarcity of available evidence. ESMO guidelines (2021) recommend comfort-directed care for those whose expected survival is less than a few weeks, noting that artificial nutrition should not be initiated at this time and that artificial hydration does not improve or prevent symptoms of thirst.

In another Cochrane review, no RCTs of the effect of medical-assisted nutrition near the end of life were identified, although megestrol was shown in another Cochrane review to be useful for improving appetite and quality of life plus slight weight gain in patients with cancer or AIDS and cachexia-anorexia syndrome.

Authors of a more recent systematic review of cachexia-anorexia syndrome found no difference in quality-of life with megestrol when compared to placebo or other active drugs despite increases in weight; there were more adverse drug effects vs, placebo, similar rates compared with active drugs, but no increase in deaths. Optimal dosing could not be determined.

Similar outcomes were observed in the most recent RCT of 190 patients with symptomatic anorexia from advanced cancer; at one-week, there was a trend towards improvement in appetite based on a numeric scale (79.3% for megestrol, 65.5% for dexamethasone, and 58.5% for placebo; p = 0.067), but no differences in performance status or QOL. Hyperglycemia and deep vein thromboses were more frequent in the dexamethasone group.

Oropharyngeal secretions: Excess secretions are common in patients at the end of life patients, with a median onset of 11-28 hours before death, and can be distressing to patients and their family and caregivers. Avoiding fluid overload and repositioning may reduce secretions. Oropharyngeal suction may actually exacerbate secretions.

Currently no high-quality data support use of anticholinergics. Commonly used medications include hyoscyamine, glycopyrrolate, scopolamine transdermal patch and atropine ophthalmic drop (1%). There is no evidence of superiority of one agent over another.
Fever: Depending on care goals and life expectancy, fever can be managed by observation or through medications such as acetaminophen, NSAIDs, or corticosteroids.

Communication is critical for ongoing patient and family support. In 1 large survey of families in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting, most were satisfied with care but 30% were dissatisfied with the information received on the cause of death and 17% felt dissatisfied with the information provided on the diagnosis.
In one RCT, use of a brochure and an end-of-life conference with families of patients dying in the ICU eased the burden of bereavement and reduced the use of nonbeneficial life-sustaining treatments.

In an RCT of structured family meetings led by palliative care specialists, however, investigators found no reduction in anxiety or depression symptoms among family surrogate decision makers in the intervention group and possibly increased posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms at 3-months post intervention. In another study, early referral to palliative care for patients with malignant pleural mesothelioma did not improve health-related QOL.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 trials found that interventions focused on improving communication and enhancing psychologic support in the ICU resulted in improvement in psychological symptoms with moderate (depression and anxiety) to very-low-certainty (post-traumatic stress) evidence in a sample of ICU surrogates facing end-of-life care decisions.

Visiting patients is an important service that family physicians provide to dying patients. In an observational videotaping study of seriously ill patients in a New York City hospital, the mean visit duration was 3 minutes for attending physicians or house officers, 2 minutes for nurses, and 24 minutes for family. Primary care providers can facilitate encounters with family and friends by offering their presence and suggestions about easing the visits (eg, reading to the patient; sharing music; creating a videotape, audiotape, or scrapbook).

Physicians should ask about and support patient and family expressions of spirituality and consider encouraging pastoral care, as desired. Spiritual support should take in account patients beliefs, values, and religious and cultural backgrounds. There is relatively little research in this area, most done in the US, and with an uncertain impact on clinical outcomes. In one study, acceptance of an offer of spiritual support was positively associated with the proposal being made by the chaplains rather than nurses (85.8% vs. 38.5%).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 4 trials concluded that patients receiving home-based end-of-life care ("hospital at home") are more likely to die at home, and there was some evidence of increased patient satisfaction at one month and reduced costs with home-based care. Home care may slightly improve patient satisfaction at one-month follow-up but not by six-months, and the effect on caregivers is uncertain.
End-of-life care in the home setting has the advantage of being more comfortable and familiar to patient. Additionally, the patient has more control over their care environment and visits.

Family caregivers were observed to engage in four phases while navigating caregiving at home for older adults at end of life, based on a synthesis of data from 24 studies. These were managing multiple roles, encountering challenges, mobilizing resources, and acknowledging that death was near.

Families usually suffer emotionally, spiritually, and financially when they care for a terminally ill patient. Twenty percent of terminally ill patients spend >10% of the family income on health care costs beyond insurance premiums and an equal percentage of caregivers stop work to provide care for a terminally ill family member. Families who need to provide care for a terminally ill patient should be made aware of community resources and the provisions in the Family Medical Leave Act.

Authors of a review of experiences and needs of parents of end-of-life palliative pediatric oncology patients found that parents felt immense guilt and a sense of failure in carrying out their parental roles. Effective communication with healthcare providers and availability of family support and religion were deemed necessary to help parents cope.

It is important that physicians ask about how caregivers are doing, and about psychological distress and the need for support. Interventions to support caregivers have been shown to reduce psychological stress in several studies. Specifically, psychosocial interventions including support groups or psychoeducation interventions for caregivers of patients with dementia, and pharmacologic interventions for the care recipient with dementia have been helpful. In this review, risk factors for caregiver burden included female sex, low educational attainment, residence with the care recipient, higher number of hours spent caregiving, depression, social isolation, financial stress, and lack of choice in being a caregiver.

Families and caregivers often need outside help, respite care, or assistance with making arrangements for the body after death. Hospice, social workers, and home health aides can offer great assistance to patients and families in addressing these needs. Funeral homes can also provide family assistance.

Children should not be excluded from the dying process of important adults around them. The physician, with permission, can help in determining what children already know about the illness and in providing accurate information about the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment expectations for the dying family member.Helpful tips include maintaining the child's daily schedule as much as possible, inquiring about school or home difficulties, informing teachers and counselors about the situation, and encouraging questions.

Hospice care refers to care provided when curative interventions have been judged to be no longer beneficial. This type of care can be delivered in many settings including home, hospital, or nursing home. Services provided include physician and nursing care, home health aides, pastoral care, counseling, respite care, and bereavement programs.

Deprescribing, especially of preventive medications, should be considered in patients at the end-of-life to avoid polypharmacy and potential complications that can result from impaired swallowing and impaired renal and hepatic function. In a RCT conducted in Spain, use of a person-centered prescription model conducted by geriatricians and clinical pharmacists with older adults admitted to a geriatric convalescence unit who required palliative care resulted in a significant reduction in the number of regular prescriptions at discharge and lower costs. Patient-oriented outcomes were not reported.

Hospice eligibility includes the following: the patient has end stage disease (eg, NYHA class IV heart disease), the patient and family prefer palliative rather than curative care, and there is documented rapid disease progression (eg, weight loss of 7.5% or 10% in the preceding 3 to 6 months, respectively, or serum albumin <2.5 g/dL) and significant functional decline. The latter can be measured with instruments like Functional Assessment Staging, Palliative Performance Scale (PPS), and Basic Activities of Daily Living.

Predicting survival is difficult. In one retrospective cohort of 590 hospice patients, Prognostat, an interactive Web-based prognostic tool, had low agreement between observed and predicted survival. The Palliative Prognosis Score was accurate in a prospective validation study. For a brief review of prognostic models, a 2014 article is available.

The Surprise Question asks "Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months?" In a systematic review of 11,621 patients from 16 observational studies, a positive response was associated with a 46% likelihood of dying in the next year, compared to only 9% in those receiving a negative response. Among patients admitted to the hospital with a COPD exacerbation, the 30-day surprise question (Would you be surprised if this patient died in the next 30 days?) had a high specificity of 95% but low sensitivity (12%) for predicting 30-day mortality. The one-year surprise question demonstrated better accuracy for predicting 1-year mortality with a specificity of 75%, sensitivity of 47%, and positive and negative predictive value of 35%, and 83%, respectively.

Among patients aged 15-29 years with cancer, the vast majority reported that prognostic information was very/extremely important at the time of diagnosis (85%), at 4 months (96%; P = .002 compared with baseline), and at 12 months (81%). Most were satisfied with prognostic disclosure over time, but desire for prognostic information increased over time. However, in an RCT of 92 patients with advanced cancer, offering life-expectancy information within a palliative-care educational intervention had no effect on patients' prognostic expectations, despite 88% of patients in the intervention group reporting that the information was important. In this study, patients' life expectancy self-estimates overall were very optimistic with 71.4% of patients with colorectal cancer estimating greater than five years and 50% of patients with pancreatic cancer estimated life expectancy greater than two years. Only 31.4% of patients reported receiving the information as upsetting, and 3.9% regretted reviewing it.

Monitoring frailty may assist in identifying patients over age 75 years at higher risk of dying who might benefit from palliative care or hospice services. In one study using monthly electronic frailty index scores available in the electronic medical record, mortality risk was increased among the 2.2% demonstrating rapid increases in frailty (OR 2.84, 95% CI 2.34-3.45) and the 21.2% demonstrating moderate increases in frailty (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.54-1.76) compared to those with stable frailty scores.

In a study of 536 patients with ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, the assessed risk scores did not have sufficient accuracy to enable decision making for triaging patients to immediate aneurysm repair, transfer or palliative care.

A model based on 2 variables, PPS score <20% and drooping of nasolabial folds, was useful in predicting impending death within 3 days for patients with advanced cancer. The PPS includes assessment of ambulation, activity and evidence of disease, self-care, intake and conscious level. Signs that have a positive likelihood ratio (LR) of 10 or more for predicting death within 3 days among cancer patients include nonreactive pupils (positive LR, 16.7; 95% CI, 14.9-18.6), an inability to close eyelids (positive LR, 13.6; 95% CI, 11.7-15.5), grunting of vocal cords (positive LR, 11.8; 95% CI, 10.3-13.4), and upper gastrointestinal bleeding (positive LR, 10.3; 95% CI, 9.5-11.1).

listitem.strong: Payment and settings for hospice services

list.listitem: In the US, the Medicare Hospice Benefit pays for 80% of all hospice care including medical, nursing, counseling, and bereavement services to terminally-ill patients and their families. To receive benefits, the patient's physician and medical director of hospice certify that the patient is terminally ill and has a life expectancy of 6 months or less if disease runs its normal course. The hospice benefit consists of two 90-day benefit periods, followed by an unlimited number of 60-day benefit periods.

There has been substantial growth in the number for-profit hospices. In one large survey of 591 Medicare-certified US hospices, for-profit hospices were somewhat less likely than nonprofit hospices to provide charity care (80% vs. 82%) and had a higher patient disenrollment rate (10% vs. 6%). For-profit hospices, however, cared for a larger proportion of patients with longer expected hospice stays including those in nursing homes (30% vs. 25%) and were more likely to engage in outreach to low-income communities (61% vs. 46%) and minority communities (59% vs. 48%).

Telehospice is a rapidly-developing approach in response to the COVID 19 pandemic. Inadequate palliative services have been reported including limited number of beds and medications to relieve symptoms.
A trial randomized 1250 patients and found that telehospice services were non-inferior to in person care.

The traditional hospice services including in-person meetings to manage patient physical, psychological and spiritual sufferings were limited by social distancing guidelines. In addition, in-person family visits were also reduced due to shortages of personal protective equipment and a desire to protect patients and staff. Fewer families were able to reach hospitals and hospice care centers and communicate with their patients or medical staff.

Many hospice patients suffered and died alone during the pandemic. Further, medical staff faced ethical dilemmas in palliative care such as decisions related to discharge planning and withdrawal of life-sustaining treatments.

According to the Association of Palliative Medicine (APM), during the pandemic shared decision making, follow up with clinical prognostic information, and support services should be provided remotely.

Remote communication tools such as smart phones and tablets can be used to deliver end-of-life services. Telehospice can positively affect the quality, cost, and accessibility of end-of-life care. In a pilot study of 14 telehealth family conferences conducted by palliative care staff, consensus on care goals related to discharge planning and withdrawal of life-sustaining treatments was reached with 13 families; satisfaction was rated as good or very good in 5 cases and the remaining 9 were neutral.

Virtual meetings can provide effective management of common physical complications including pain and constipation in addition, to providing other support like friendship calls, live storytelling, live craft, art and baking sessions.

Telehealth resources are available on the websites of the American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine (AAHPM), National Hospice and Palliative Care Organization (NHPCO), American Medical Association (AMA), and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).
Building infrastructures to establish access for telehealth specialists is one of the Colorado’s Priorities for COVID-19 Palliative and Hospice Care Surge Planning.

The APM released 2020 guidelines for COVID-19 and Palliative, End of Life and Bereavement Care in Secondary Care. It provides flowcharts to deal with severe end-of-life symptoms that could arise from COVID 19 infection

Processes that many dying persons go through include social withdrawal, decreased senses (hearing is the most persistent), increased sleep, restlessness, disorientation (redirect the patient only if distressed), and decreasing nutritional requirements. With respect to nutrition, forced feeding should be discouraged. In elderly patients with dementia, tube feeding provides no clinical benefit. Authors of a Cochrane review of 5 small RCTs found insufficient evidence to support use of music therapy in end-of-life care.

Incontinence of urine and bowel movements is often not a problem until death is very near. Absorbent pads can be placed under the patient for greater comfort and cleanliness or a urinary catheter can be used for comfort care.

Physical changes to expect include flushing, bluish hue to the skin, and cold or clammy skin. As circulation decreases, the hands and feet become purplish and skin appears blotchy. Blood pressure decreases, the pulse may increase or decrease, body temperature can fluctuate, and respirations may increase, decrease, or become irregular with periods of apnea.

Congestion can present as a rattling sound in the lungs and/or upper throat because the patient is too weak to clear secretions. No particular intervention has been found helpful, including atropine, hyoscine hydrobromide, and hyoscine butylbromide, and glycopyrronium. Simple position change and avoidance of fluid overload can be considered.
Guidance on withdrawal of life support is provided in an ACP ethics manual.

Evidence-based criteria for withdrawing life support is lacking; however, general consensus exists based on ethical and clinical principles in the care of these patients. Withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment should be considered when cure is not possible and treatment is no longer desired and does not provide comfort to patients. Important steps include informed consent, appropriate setting and monitoring, sedation and analgesia, emotional support for families, and documentation. In 1 study, slower withdrawal of life support for ICU patients with longer stays and extubation before death were associated with higher levels of family satisfaction.

In a systematic review of 15 articles, staggered patterns of withdrawal of life-support therapy were reported, with vasoactive drugs withdrawn first followed by gradual withdrawal of mechanical ventilation; the process of therapy withdrawal, however, did not appear to influence time to death.
Family presence during brain death evaluation in one study improved understanding of the death with no apparent adverse effect on psychological well-being.

Physician-assisted death, also called physician-assisted suicide (PAS), is legal in the Netherlands, Belgium, Canada (2016) and in the states of California, Colorado, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maine, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Vermont, and Washington (data from 2020).
Few patients actually consider PAS and patients who request it should be advised of the extent to which palliative care can provide relief.
At this time, the ACP does not support PAS or euthanasia.

Determination of Death: Determining death is legally accepted when all brain functions achieve irreversible cessation. Medical support devices should be usually discontinued in patients who meet the brain death criteria.

Following the death of the patient, personal expressions of condolence from the primary care provider(s) and staff should be encouraged such as sending condolence cards and attending the funeral; based on personal experience, the latter can assist with grieving and closure for the physician. Follow-up is important to support family members with grief and bereavement.

Authors of a systematic review of 46 articles found hospital bereavement practices included memorial services, letters, and services provided by bereavement coordinators. Bereavement practices employed by medical providers included answering or making phone calls, attending family meetings, and sending condolence letters. Among general practice practitioners, 71% reported attendance at a patient's funeral.

feature.caption: Options for the Management of Common Problems at the End of Life.

tr.td: Pain
Massage, positioning, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, physical therapy, chiropractic therapy, acupuncture, hypnosis, spiritual practices, prayer

Nonopioids (eg, acetaminophen 4 g/d, ibuprofen 1600 mg/d), advanced to mild opioids (eg, codeine 30 mg every 4 hours or hydrocodone 5 mg every 4 hours), or stronger opioids (eg, morphine 5-10 mg every 4 hours), as needed; calcitonin; antidepressants; anticonvulsants; nerve blocks; radiotherapy; radiofrequency ablation
Constipation
Increasing fiber and fluids; increasing activity

Stool softeners (eg, sodium docusate 300-600 mg/d oral); stimulant laxatives (eg, prune juice 1/2-1 glass/d, senna 2-4 tablet/d, bisacodyl 5-15 mg/d orally or per rectum); osmotic laxatives (eg, lactulose 15-30 mL every 4 to 8 hours, magnesium hydroxide 15-30 mL/d)
Dyspnea
Pulmonary rehabilitation
Opioids (eg, codeine 30 mg every 4 hours, morphine 5-10 mg every 4 hours); anxiolytics (eg, lorazepam 0.5-2 mg oral/sublingual/IV, diazepam 5-10 mg oral/IV)
Fatigue
Decreasing or increasing activity; discontinuing or changing medications; reducing sleep disturbances; acupuncture
Glucocorticoids (eg, dexamethasone 2-4 mg per day); stimulants (eg, dextroamphetamine 5-10 mg oral up 20 mg); modafinil 100-200 mg up to 400 mg/day
Depression
Counseling; exercise; music therapy
Antidepressant medications (eg, fluoxetine 10 mg/d and increase as needed); psychostimulants (eg, dextroamphetamine or methylphenidate 2.5-5 mg twice daily) if rapid onset of action needed
Delirium
Gentle reassurance; reorientation; safety precautions; aide presence; reducing medications

Neuroleptic (eg, haloperidol 0.5-5 mg oral/subcutaneous/IM/IV every 1-4 hours, risperidone 1-3 mg every 12 hours); anxiolytic (eg, lorazepam 0.5-2 mg oral/IM/IV); anesthetic (propofol 0.3-2 mg/hour continuous infusion)
Anorexia/cachexia
Eating with family members; taste of food helpful
Progestogens for cancer patients (eg, megestrol acetate 400-800 mg); corticosteroids (eg, dexamethasone up to 4 mg/day)
Dehydration
Offer ice chips and small amounts of fluid as tolerated; lubricate lips
Hypodermoclysis (subcutaneous infusion of fluids)
Nausea and vomiting (late stage)
High protein meals with ginger; acupuncture point stimulation wristband

Metoclopramide 20 mg or 0.5 mg/kg orally; scopolamine patch every 72 hours; promethazine 25 mg oral or rectal every 4-6 hours or 12.5-25 mg IV/IM every 4-6 hours; diphenhydramine 25-50 mg oral/IM/IV every 4-6 hours; 5-HT3 blockers (eg, ondansetron 8 mg or 0.15 mg/kg IV once, prechemotherapy and 16-24 mg orally once, prechemotherapy); aprepitant, acute: 125 mg orally once, prechemotherapy
